decision.explanation: On the paraboloid, the outward vector area element is ⟨2x,2y,1⟩ dA, giving F·dS=[-2x(5-x²-y²)+x] dA. The bottom disk has outward normal ⟨0,0,-1⟩ and contributes -x dA. Adding gives 2x³+2xy²-10x, option b. All displayed expressions integrate to zero by symmetry, but b directly represents the combined surface contributions.

Consider the vector field $F=⟨-z,\,0,\,x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
after.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So, 

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper paraboloid ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=-z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-5,\,Q=0,\,R=x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-5)\cdot (-2x)-0\cdot (-2y)+x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-10x+x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-9x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨-z,0,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-9x)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-10x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Consider the vector field F=⟨−z,0,x⟩ and the closed surface S that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let D be the projection of S onto the xy-plane. The flux of F across S can be expressed in terms of a double integral as ∬SF⋅dS=∬DAAAAAAAdA. Which of the following could be the missing expression?

a
4x3−4xy2+10x
b
2x3+2xy2−10x
c
−2x3−6xy2−6x
d
2x3+4xy2−6x
e
−4x3−2xy2+6x
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

  • the upper surface S1:z=g(x,y)=5−x2−y2 is oriented upward, and

  • the lower surface S2:z=h(x,y)=0 is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

  • Consider the upper paraboloid S1.

    We compute the partial derivatives of z=g(x,y): ∂g∂x=∂∂x(5−x2−y2)=−2x∂g∂y=∂∂y(5−x2−y2)=−2y

    If we denote F=⟨P,Q,R⟩, then P=−z=x2+y2−5,Q=0,R=x.

    As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have ∬S1F⋅dS=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=∬D−(x2+y2−5)⋅(−2x)−0⋅(−2y)+xdA=∬D2x3+2xy2−10x+xdA=∬D2x3+2xy2−9xdA.

  • Consider the lower plane S2.

    Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is n=⟨0,0,−1⟩. As a result, we have ∬S2F⋅dS=∬S2F⋅ndS=∬D⟨−z,0,x⟩⋅⟨0,0,−1⟩dA=∬D−xdA.

Therefore, the flux of F across the entire surface is ∬SF⋅dS=∬S1F⋅dS+∬S2F⋅dS=∬D(2x3+2xy2−9x)dA+∬D−xdA=∬D2x3+2xy2−10xdA.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094681/assets/0e374f18d8b87de2fddd9a2127ee84709746c7c1b75083441afcc7b6c79402fb.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨-z,\,0,\,x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
content.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So, 

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper paraboloid ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=-z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-5,\,Q=0,\,R=x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-5)\cdot (-2x)-0\cdot (-2y)+x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-10x+x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-9x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨-z,0,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-9x)\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{x}^{3}+2x{y}^{2}-10x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Let r=√(x²+y²). For the upper cone z=3-r, the outward vector area element is ⟨x/r,y/r,1⟩ dA. Its dot product with F=⟨0,-x,-z⟩ is -xy/r+r-3. The bottom disk contributes zero because z=0. Thus b directly gives the missing expression. The other choices also integrate to zero over the symmetric disk, but b follows the surface-flux calculation.

Consider the vector field $F=⟨0,\,-x,\,-z⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
after.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So, 

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=3-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper cone ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=0,\,Q=-x,\,R=-z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-0\cdot (-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})-(-x)\cdot (-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨0,-x,-0⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}0\,\text{d}A \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A+0 \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

  • the upper surface S1:z=g(x,y)=3−x2+y2 is oriented upward, and

  • the lower surface S2:z=h(x,y)=0 is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

  • Consider the upper cone S1.

    We compute the partial derivatives of z=g(x,y): ∂g∂x=∂∂x(3−x2+y2)=−xx2+y2∂g∂y=∂∂y(3−x2+y2)=−yx2+y2

    If we denote F=⟨P,Q,R⟩, then P=0,Q=−x,R=−z=x2+y2−3.

    As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have ∬S1F⋅dS=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=∬D−0⋅(−xx2+y2)−(−x)⋅(−yx2+y2)+x2+y2−3dA=∬D−xyx2+y2+x2+y2−3dA.

Consider the vector field $F=⟨0,\,-x,\,-z⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
content.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So, 

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=3-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=0$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper cone ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3-\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=0,\,Q=-x,\,R=-z=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-0\cdot (-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})-(-x)\cdot (-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨0,-x,-0⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}0\,\text{d}A \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux of $F$ across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A+0 \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-3\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field F=⟨z,0,x⟩ and the closed surface S that encloses the finite region between the paraboloid z=9−x2−y2 and the plane z=1. Let D be the projection of S onto the xy-plane. The flux of F across S can be expressed in terms of a double integral as ∬SF⋅dS=∬DAAAAAAAdA. Which of the following could be the missing expression?

a
 16x−xy2+2y2
b
 20x+2yx3−2xy2
c
 19x−2x3+3y2
d
 20x+x3−2xy2
e
18x−2x3−2xy2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

  • the upper surface S1:z=g(x,y)=9−x2−y2 is oriented upward, and

  • the lower surface S2:z=h(x,y)=1 is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

  • Consider the upper paraboloid S1.

    We compute the partial derivatives of z=g(x,y): ∂g∂x=∂∂x(9−x2−y2)=−2x∂g∂y=∂∂y(9−x2−y2)=−2y

    If we denote F=⟨P,Q,R⟩, then P=z=9−x2−y2,Q=0,R=x.

    As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have ∬S1F⋅dS=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=∬D(−(9−x2−y2)⋅(−2x)−(0)⋅(−2y)+x)dA=∬D(18x−2x3−2xy2+x)dA=∬D19x−2x3−2xy2dA.

  • Consider lower plane S2.

    Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is n=⟨0,0,−1⟩. As a result, we have ∬S2F⋅dS=∬S2F⋅ndS=∬D⟨z,0,x⟩⋅⟨0,0,−1⟩dA=∬D−xdA.

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is

∬SF⋅dS=∬S1F⋅dS+∬S2F⋅dS=∬D19x−2x3−2xy2dA+∬D−xdA=∬D18x−2x3−2xy2dA.

content.problem:
Consider the vector field $F=⟨z,\,0,\,x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the paraboloid $z=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the plane $z=1.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
content.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=1$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper paraboloid ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=z=9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,Q=0,\,R=x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot (-2x)-(0)\cdot (-2y)+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(18x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}19x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is downward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,-1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨z,0,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,-1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}19x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}18x-2{x}^{3}-2x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Writing g=√(4-x²-y²), the upper hemisphere has outward vector area element ⟨x/g,y/g,1⟩ dA, giving flux integrand xy/g+y. The lower plane has downward vector area element ⟨-1/2,0,-1⟩ dA, giving -y. Their sum is xy/g, option c.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Consider the vector field $F=⟨0,\,x,\,y⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the hemisphere $z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ and the plane $z=1-\frac{1}{2}x.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
after.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=1-\frac{1}{2}x$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper hemisphere ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=0,\,Q=x,\,R=y.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-0\cdot (-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})-x\cdot (-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{xy}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-\frac{1}{2}x)=-\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-\frac{1}{2}x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=0,\,Q=x,\,R=y.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-0\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})-x\cdot 0+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{xy}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+y)\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the vector field F=⟨0,x,y⟩ and the closed surface S that encloses the finite region between the hemisphere z=4−x2−y2 and the plane z=1−12x. Let D be the projection of S onto the xy-plane. The flux of F across S can be expressed in terms of a double integral as ∬SF⋅dS=∬DAAAAAAAdA. Which of the following could be the missing expression?

a
 xy4−x2−y2+y
b
 xy+y4−x2−y2
c
 xy4−x2−y2
d
 y−xy4−x2−y2
e
 y4−x2−y2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

  • the upper surface S1:z=g(x,y)=4−x2−y2 is oriented upward, and

  • the lower surface S2:z=h(x,y)=1−12x is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

  • Consider the upper hemisphere S1.

    We compute the partial derivatives of z=g(x,y): ∂g∂x=∂∂x(4−x2−y2)=−x4−x2−y2∂g∂y=∂∂y(4−x2−y2)=−y4−x2−y2

    If we denote F=⟨P,Q,R⟩, then P=0,Q=x,R=y.

    As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have ∬S1F⋅dS=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=∬D(−0⋅(−x4−x2−y2)−x⋅(−y4−x2−y2)+y)dA=∬D(xy4−x2−y2+y)dA.

  • Consider lower plane S2.

    We compute the partial derivatives of z=h(x,y): ∂h∂x=∂∂x(1−12x)=−12∂h∂y=∂∂y(1−12x)=0

    If we denote F=⟨P,Q,R⟩, then P=0,Q=x,R=y.

    As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have ∬S2F⋅dS=−∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=−∬D(−0⋅(−12)−x⋅0+y)dA=−∬DydA.

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is

∬SF⋅dS=∬S1F⋅dS+∬S2F⋅dS=∬D(xy4−x2−y2+y)dA−∬DydA=∬Dxy4−x2−y2dA.

content.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux as a Double Integral
content.problem:
Consider the vector field $F=⟨0,\,x,\,y⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the hemisphere $z=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ and the plane $z=1-\frac{1}{2}x.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
content.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=1-\frac{1}{2}x$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper hemisphere ${S}_{1}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=0,\,Q=x,\,R=y.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is upward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-0\cdot (-\frac{x}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})-x\cdot (-\frac{y}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}})+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{xy}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider lower plane ${S}_{2}.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-\frac{1}{2}x)=-\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-\frac{1}{2}x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=0,\,Q=x,\,R=y.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-0\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})-x\cdot 0+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{xy}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+y)\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Correct
EXPLANATION

Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

  • the upper surface S1:z=g(x,y)=0 is oriented upward, and

  • the lower surface S2:z=h(x,y)=x2+y2−4 is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

  • Consider the upper plane S1.

    Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is n=⟨0,0,1⟩. As a result, we have ∬S1F⋅dS=∬S1F⋅ndS=∬D⟨y,0,x⟩⋅⟨0,0,1⟩dA=∬DxdA.

  • Consider the lower paraboloid S2.

    We compute the partial derivatives of z=h(x,y): ∂h∂x=∂∂x(x2+y2−4)=2x∂h∂y=∂∂y(x2+y2−4)=2y

    If we denote F=⟨P,Q,R⟩, then P=y,Q=0,R=x.

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is ∬SF⋅dS=∬S1F⋅dS+∬S2F⋅dS=∬DxdA+∬D2xy−xdA=∬D2xydA.

$$
